Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What are some things that everyone needs to unlearn?
Answer: Here are 5 common life lessons that most people would better off unlearning. As you can see, I’m a very serious pajama fighter, so I know lots of things about life. Thing to unlearn #1: Your “happiness” is the most important thing in your life. Not only is “happiness” not the most important thing in your life, the American definition of happiness kind of sucks. It’s self-centered, it’s self-serving, and for whatever reason, it’s also something that our culture is obsessed with. However, in America, when you try to make yourself happier, you actually become less happy and more disconnected. Other cultures have different definitions of happiness, meaning that for different people around the world, different actions are taken to improve life satisfaction. One definition that I like is a popular Japanese concept called “Ikigai”. Ikigai is the intersection between achievement, collectivity, personal satisfaction, and altruism. To me, it seems more holistic and less destructive that the American “pursuit of happiness” which seems to require a great deal of suffering to achieve. I believe that the more you pursue happiness, the harder it becomes to find. Thing to unlearn #2: Working hard in silence is how you “make it in life”. When I decided that I wanted to become a Jiu-Jitsu athlete, I began an intense daily training regimen that I have kept up for more than 6 years at this point. Nearly every day has had either drilling, sparring, strength training, technical study, or all of the above. At the very least, I think about how I can get better at grappling every single day. For years, instead of telling anyone about how hard I was pushing myself, I just kept working until I was at my breaking point, and then I kept going. “Suffer in silence,” I thought, channeling my inner Muhammad Ali, “one day your work will do the talking for you.” Your work never talks for you, and people who tell you that are compensating for being bad at expressing themselves. You have to speak up for yourself, it’s the only way to do it. Working hard in silence is not a path to greatness, it’s a path to isolation, depression, and feeling forgotten. The irony is that the people telling you that they are working hard in silence are not working in silence. You wouldn’t hear them if they really were. Just talk about what you do. It’s cool. We want to hear about it. Thing to unlearn #3: Failure isn’t final, but success IS final. The movie doesn’t end when you lose and it doesn’t end when you win. The movie ends when you die. But even then, it just keeps going for everyone else. I keep signing up for these Jiu-Jitsu tournaments and writing these articles that go viral (I wrote something that in May hit 2.5 million views!), and no matter what I do, none of the success has made me “set”. I never feel at peace with my effort. There’s always another mountain to climb. No matter what I do, there’s more work to do to get to where I want to be in my life. This isn’t just because I’m young, it’s because I operate from a mindset that I am not satisfied with where I’m at and that I have to improve. I’m still hungry. You’re never going to get to the top of the mountain, and because of that, you have to decide when you’re going to stop climbing. Even after you win a world championship, set a new PR at the gym, get a girlfriend, get your black belt, or write something that you’re proud of that lots of people read, there’s more work to do. The problem isn’t the work, the problem is that you are looking at the work as a temporary sacrifice to get to a destination. The work is the destination. Thing to unlearn #4: You are a “product” of your environment. You are not inherently a product of the 5 people you spend the most time with. You are not inherently a product of your environment. You are not a product. You are a person. I guess I should save the rant about the commodification of self for another time, but people really get really hung up on finding for themselves the perfect routine, the perfect diet, and the perfect life because they want to optimize their experience. They want to maximize their meat suit. Doing this sacrifices some unique about the human experience. Trying to become a “homo Deus” distorts your experience as a homo sapien. This is inevitable. I’m not saying you shouldn't try to live a great life, I’m just saying that maybe there’s more to life than trying to optimize your optimizations. I’m saying that you have to decide how much optimization you want to go for because every action has consequences. “Your body is not a temple, it’s an amusement park. Enjoy the ride.”― Anthony Bourdain Thing to unlearn #5: Your life needs to be balanced to be happy. I’ve never met any great athletes who are “balanced people”. All the best athletes that I know all work tirelessly toward their goals, alienate people, sacrifice joy for their fulfillment, and grind for wins as their life depends on it. In high-level athletics, anything less than everything you’ve got will leave you short of your potential. Sacrificing this balance is the price of being an athlete, and I believe the same is true in other endeavors. The life of an athlete is not balanced. The sensations that athletes deal with include constant exhaustion, chronic physical pain, and the anxiety of not knowing what their next move is going to be. The life of an athlete is exciting and scary and a little bit like a choose-your-own-adventure book, but it is not balanced. I know because this is my life, and while I love it, I won’t be able to do it forever. My body won’t allow it. One day, I’ll have to live a balanced life, but that day hasn’t come yet. I love what I’m doing right now, but I don’t see myself doing this at the same level in a decade. In 5–15 years, depending on my health, success, and mindset, I will probably live a different life. Maybe I will have balance then, but I will only know that it’s balanced because I am imbalanced right now. Peace has a price. Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: What is freedom?
Answer: Today is the 4th of July (Independence Day in America), so I thought I’d write a little about what I think freedom is. In America, we make a big fuss about having “freedom”, but we still use smartphones that basically listen to all of our conversations (I see you, targeted Instagram ads). We make a big fuss about having freedom, but recently we overturned the freedom for a woman to have an abortion. We say “freedom ain’t free”, but honestly, neither are we. What America does well is provide its citizens with the illusion of freedom. To me, freedom means that I and my family have as equal opportunities for a life of prosperity as other people. I’m a white guy, so I’ve kind of got it easy. I’ve got a lot of freedom. It’d be silly for me to stand up on a soapbox and talk about unfree I am. Most of my shackles are mental. Other people aren’t so lucky. In America, we have this thing called systemic racism. You’ve probably heard of it. Maybe your country has it too. Basically, it means that people of other races do not have access to the same schools, the same safe neighborhoods, or the same healthcare. I’m simplifying a bit, but follow along. Let’s look at my hometown of Chicago for a second so that you can see what I mean. In Chicago, we have a black female lesbian mayor right now. The first black American president came from Chicago. Nonetheless, the systemic racism in Chicago runs very deep. Historically black communities in Chicago do not have as many schools, grocery stores, or police officers (though the Chicago Police Department does have a lengthy history of racist behavior, so more police probably wouldn’t help these black neighborhoods) as more wealthy communities. Schools in historically black communities are more likely to be shut down than schools in predominantly white neighborhoods. Communities in Chicago that are historically black never have gotten the outside help that they needed when they were first formed, and as a result, they’ve struggled to keep up with other communities in terms of property value. Because of this, the communities are valued less than the wealthier neighborhoods. The result of this compounded over decades is that historically black communities are less safe, there is less opportunity for growth, and worst of all, it’s very hard for people to leave. To put it bluntly, Chicago is more dangerous right now than it's ever been, and little is being done about it because the sources of the danger primarily are in communities that have a lower value. Using the definition of freedom that I used in the opening of this piece, it’s hard to say that these communities are “free”. Today there was a mass shooting in a Suburban town called Highland Park, just a few miles north of Chicago. It was a devastating event that made national news. At the same time, there have been more than 971 shootings in Chicago this year already. I haven’t seen much in the news about that. Even more tragic is that this number is down from the pandemic. It’s really hard to stand over people and tell them to dig their way out of a hole that they didn’t put themselves in when they don’t even have a shovel. So yes, freedom exists in America. You can say pretty much whatever you want besides yelling “fire” in a crowded theatre or whatever. But at the same time, your freedom is more dictated by the things that you have than the things that you don’t. It’s tough to say that a grocery store clerk living in West Garfield Park has the same amount of freedom as a CEO living in Streeterville (an upscale neighborhood in Chicago). You can say what you want and you can vote for whoever you want, but this doesn’t make you free. These rights give you the illusion of freedom. On the 4th of July, we don’t celebrate freedom. We celebrate the thought that we are free. For a lot of people, this is good enough.

Name: Chris Wojcik
Question: Why do men with goals succeed in life and men without goals fail?
Answer: It’s not really “men with goals” versus “men without goals”. It’s “people with goals” versus “people without goals”. Obviously, “having goals” alone isn’t enough to be successful, but it’s a great start. We’ll talk more about that in a minute. To me, the guy in this picture looks like he’s trying to focus on his goals. But does he look happy? Goals alone won’t make you happy, but they can make you unhappy. If you don’t have goals, you can’t fail or succeed. You’re just existing. You’re like a blob with arms and legs floating through the multidimensional plane of existence. And actually, in terms of spirtual health, that might be a really great thing. Men with goals can succeed, but men without goals are probably a lot lower in anxiety and stress. It’s hard to stress out about stuff when nothing matters. One of my old childhood friends has no goals. He seems pretty content, but his life has stagnated in terms of progress. That’s his choice. He doesn’t have the high highs or the low lows I have, but he gets by okay. You’d have to ask him how he finds meaning in his existence. I, on the other hand, feel that goals are essential to meaning. To me, it seems that without goals, my life is essentially meaningless. At the same time, I am self-aware enough to know that “having goals” alone is not going to make my life complete. This is the dichotomy of goal-setting: Having goals can make you happy, but it might also make you sad if those goals don’t work out. Not having goals means you won’t get sad, but you also might not get happy. To put it another way, either you create meaning in your life, or your life is meaningless. I used to struggle a lot with nihilism. Perks of being raised without religion, I guess. I never believed in a higher power or anything like that, and I never believed that anything in my life was objectively meaningful. For the longest time, I thought that this meant that my life was meaningless. Because I thought it, it was so. This was my reality from 12–21, I was very depressed about it. I fought the feelings of meaninglessness, but they were persistent. I did stuff in my life, but the stuff I did didn’t matter to me. I couldn’t handle failing, so I decided that not having goals would have been safer. I never said that I wanted to be a Jiu-Jitsu world champion because wanting to be champion meant that not being a champion would be failure. I’d have rather not tried and not failed than not tried. It made me miserable. Even worse, because I wasn’t “all-in”, the results of my pursuits were always mediocre, and I was very unhappy. I was too scared to be anything, so I was nothing. Men (people) without goals cannot be anything. This is why they don’t succeed. This is why many of them are miserable. This, I believe, is the route of modern nihilism. It’s not a lack of success that makes us unhappy, but a lack of hope. Learn to be a happy failure. Let’s talk about people with goals. People who have created meaning in their lives. People who want to live better. People who want to try to be happy—like, really happy (I’m not talking about peace here, I’m not talking about joy). If you don’t try to be happy, you can’t be happy. If you don’t try to succeed, you can’t succeed. This is simple, but most people don’t let this idea sink in. Once you have “goals”—your personal antidote to nihilism—then you can begin to live a life that has more meaning and more purpose. You can make art. You can build meaningful connections (with people who have similar personal visions). You can live and work and succeed. That’s why goals matter. Goals give you a framework to create a meaningful life. That’s also why it’s so important to choose goals that are aligned with your personal values. If your value is helping people, you probably won’t get a lot of meaning out of trying to chase money or status. Setting the goal of making a butt-ton of money because a motivation YouTube video told you to would be stupid and it would make you unhappy. Choose goals that matter to you. When your “hustle” gives your life meaning, it doesn’t feel like a hustle anymore. It feels like living. Either way, you’re going to die one day. You might as well do some shit before your time comes. The potential upside is limited only by your imagination.

Question: Can you make money from a blog?
Answer: I’ve been blogging for almost 18 months now. Here are 5 blogging lessons that I wished I’d learned sooner. To answer your question: yes, you can make money from a blog. However, you probably won’t.  Most blogs do not make much money. I make a few hundred per month on Medium. I make like 20 bucks per month on Quora. I make about $30 per month with my premium newsletter. My blogging/digital writing alone is not enough for me to live and do cool stuff. It’s just not. I also write 6–7 days per week, publish writing nearly every day, and I have done so for nearly a year. I make more than most writers on Medium (and I’m a top writer in a few categories), but I am still not making a living. That’s not to dissuade you. I’m just saying, if you think this is going to be easy, you’re in for an unpleasant surprise. It’s hard as fuck — especially if writing is not a passion for you. Don’t start blogging for the money, the money is only there for the most popular blogs. Popularity comes through consistently.  You won’t strike gold, but you might build it. I had beginner's luck on Medium. I went viral after just a few months, and I thought that that meant I was going to be a famous writer and everyone was going to love me. I was an idiot. After the virality ends, you have 2 choices: 1. You can go viral again, and spend your career going from viral hit to viral hit. 2. Or, you can slowly but surely build a consistent, loyal audience over years and years of consistent writing. Going viral is exciting, but viruses don’t stay in your system forever. That’s a good thing. Build an audience slowly by putting your best foot forward every single day. — it’s better that way. Don’t strive to be a one-hit-wonder.  No platform is safe. Get over it. It seems like every other week, I see an article on Medium, an answer on Quora, a post on LinkedIn, or a tweet about how each of those platforms is “dying” and how you can’t make money on them anymore. People are saying this, but plenty of people are still making hundreds of dollars per month with each platform. Yes, it’s possible that Medium could turn into the MySpace of writing, but is it likely? I don’t think so. I think people just like saying that the sky is falling. It’s already insanely difficult to get good at writing. Writing on Medium is a separate skill in itself. Don’t waste your limited writing energy by complaining about your lack of views, lack of earnings, or how “the platform sucks”. Just write shit. Then, write more shit. You’re welcome in advance.  If no one’s reading your work, the only person you can blame is yourself. Sorry for the tough love, but some bloggers need it. The entitlement in the blogging world is ridiculous. When people don’t get views, they usually blame everyone and everything but themselves. I’ve been seeing this since I started on here. Writers blame their mom for being in the room with them while they're writing (not exaggerating — I’ve seen it). They blame the publication for publishing their article at the wrong time of day. They blame the platform (like I said in the last point) for sucking at making their stories go viral. Have you ever thought that maybe, just maybe, no one read your article because your article wasn’t that great? Even if the algorithm does suck, the story that you tell yourself will determine much of your success. Accept personal responsibility, and keep striving to do better work. This isn’t toxic advice, this is the only advice that will allow you to stick with writing long enough to do it will. A great way to test the validity of your ideas is to post the same article in multiple places. Repurpose your ideas as tweets, Quora answers, LinkedIn posts, and Medium articles/blog posts. If the idea doesn’t perform on all of these platforms, there’s really only one thing to blame, and it’s not the algorithm. Learning to blame yourself without hating yourself is the secret sauce to continued progress.  Every niche is saturated. Be yourself.
